items.text: Do not sell or give away the ancestral land without your sons' consent; dispose of only a reasonable part of it.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Chapter VI: Inheritance § 1.: Antiquities
items.quote: the father, for example, could not sell or give away the ancestral land without the consent of his sons, or could only dispose of some 'reasonable' part of it.

items.text: Do good works for the good of your ancestor's soul, as the church preaches.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, VI.1
items.quote: Much might be done by a pious heir for the good of his ancestor’s soul, and the duty of doing this was sedulously preached
items.conflict: Prayers for the dead; salvation by faith alone

items.text: Acknowledge your younger brothers' moral claims to share in the family inheritance, even when the law makes you the sole heir.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance §2
items.quote: gradually the claims of the younger sons upon their eldest brother may become merely moral claims which the king’s court does not enforce.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Do not contradict what the dead man said at the last; let his words stand by two or three witnesses.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol.2, VI.3
items.quote: in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established, for perchance the avarice of the kinsfolk of the dead would contradict what was said

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 1.: Antiquities

items.text: Forsake your own people and your father's house, and be subject to your husband as your head.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. 6, § 1
items.quote: the husband is the head of the wife, that the wife must forsake her own people and her father’s house

items.text: Avenge the death of your slain kinsman.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. 6, § 1
items.quote: those who are bound and entitled to avenge his death
items.conflict: Vengeance belongs to God (Rom 12:19); private blood-feud is not for Christians.

items.text: Find a lord for your lordless kinsman.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. 6, § 1
items.quote: when the ‘kindred’ of a lordless man is ordered to find him a lord

items.text: As a paternal kinsman, guard the paternal goods of a fatherless child.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. 6, § 1
items.quote: the guardianship however of its paternal goods is given by ancient dooms to its paternal kinsmen

items.text: Bring up a fatherless child among its maternal kin.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. 6, § 1
items.quote: this child will be brought up among its maternal, not its paternal, kinsmen

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 1.: Antiquities

items.text: Honor your mother's brother as you honor your father.
items.citation: History of English Law before Edward I, vol. 2, Inheritance, Antiquities
items.quote: Sororum filiis idem apud avunculum qui apud patrem honor. — A sister's son holds the same honor with his maternal uncle as with his father.

items.text: When a kinsman slays a man, bear the wergild: paternal kin pay two parts, maternal kin pay one part.
items.citation: History of English Law before Edward I, vol. 2, Inheritance, Antiquities
items.quote: if the slayer has both paternal and maternal kinsfolk, the paternal pay two-thirds, the maternal one-third

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Do not claim a share in land held by military service; it descends whole to the eldest son.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, VI.2
items.quote: land held by military service is impartible

items.text: If the father held partible socage land, divide it equally among yourselves; let no son take more than his brother.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, VI.2
items.quote: the estates which according to Glanvill are partible, are only the estates of the 'free sokemen'

items.text: When dividing the father's house, reserve the hearth for the youngest son.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, VI.2
items.quote: When his father’s house has to be divided, the hearth (astre) is reserved for him.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 1.: Antiquities

items.text: Do not alienate inherited book-land outside the kindred if the original grant forbade it.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.VI.1
items.quote: he is not to alienate it outside his kindred, if there is writing or witness that this was forbidden

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Recognize the eldest sister as head of the inheritance and hold your share of her, not of the overlord directly.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: they will “achieve” (accapitare) to her, that is, will recognize her as their head

items.text: The third heir in a younger sister's line must pay relief and become the man of the eldest sister or her heir.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: the third heir of Barbara or Clara must pay relief to, and become the man of, Alice or her heir
items.needs_role: third heir in a younger sister's line; heir of the eldest sister

items.text: Do not claim the marriage or wardship of your younger sisters; those rights belong to the overlord, not to the eldest co-heiress.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: The eldest daughter, the writ says, is not to have the marriage and wardship of her sisters

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Do not alienate your land without the consent of your expectant heirs unless it is a case of necessity; and even then give them an opportunity to purchase it.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: must not alienate his land without the consent of his expectant heirs unless it be a case of necessity

items.text: Do not alienate your wife's land as if it were your own; seek her consent and preserve her inheritance.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: when a husband had been alienating his wife’s land

items.text: Honor your father's warranty: do not claim the land he covenanted to warrant away.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: Baldwin is rebutted from the claim by his ancestor’s warranty.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Provide for his brothers to the best of his ability.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii, VI.2
items.quote: he was bound to provide for his brothers to the best of his ability

items.text: Do not make one expectant heir better off than another; a father's gift of land to one son is undone by death.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii, VI.2
items.quote: no one is to make one of his expectant heirs better off than the rest

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Reserve for your wife the aliquot share that custom secures to her from your estate.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3.: The Last Will
items.quote: the custom which secured an aliquot share to the wife

items.text: Reserve for your children the aliquot share that custom secures to them from your estate.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3.: The Last Will
items.quote: an aliquot share to the children

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Do not insist that the sole house fall to your share; let it be physically divided among the co-heiresses unless all agree otherwise.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: if there was but one house, the eldest daughter had no right to insist that this should fall to her share... the house itself was physically divided.

items.text: If you take an indivisible inheritance such as a castle or the head of a barony, account for its value to your sisters in the division of the rest.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: a castle could not be partitioned, nor the messuage which was the head of a barony. This passed as a whole to the eldest of the sisters, but she accounted for its value

items.text: Do not claim the first presentation to a benefice for yourself; join with your sisters in a joint presentation, or it will lapse to the ordinary.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: if there was but one advowson, the eldest sister could not claim the first presentation as her own; all the parceners must join in a presentation

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Observe your father's testamentary distribution of his goods, as he charged you.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, ii, ch. 6, § 3
items.quote: he charges his sons to observe this distribution

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Do not utterly disinherit your expectant heir.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: he must not utterly disinherit the expectant heir.

items.text: Treat your sons as equals; give no one of them preference over the others.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: a father ought not to give one of his sons a preference over the others; they are equals and should be treated as equals.

items.text: Obtain your eldest son's consent before giving any part of your heritage to a younger son.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.2
items.quote: Without the consent of his eldest son he can 'hardly' give any part of his heritage to a younger son.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Refrain from self-help and legal action if the uncle has first obtained seisin; the casus Regis bars you.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Book II, Ch. VI, § 2
items.quote: the nephew must not have recourse to self-help, nor has he any action by which he can obtain a judgment.

items.text: Give up the land to the nephew, for he is the rightful heir, when he brings his writ of right.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Book II, Ch. VI, § 2
items.quote: The nephew can now recover the land from the uncle by writ of right although the uncle was the first to get seisin.

items.text: Do not seek to inherit from your deceased child; the law bars ascendants.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Book II, Ch. VI, § 2
items.quote: neither my father, nor my mother, nor any remoter ancestor can be my heir

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Provide for your younger sons in your lifetime, since only the eldest will inherit.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.VI.2
items.quote: a father must in his lifetime provide for his younger sons, if he wishes them to be provided for at all.

items.text: If you become lord of the land, surrender it to your younger brother rather than hold both seignory and tenancy.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.VI.2
items.quote: he must not be both lord and heir. Having become lord, he must give up the land to C.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 1.: Antiquities

items.text: Pay the debts of your departed ancestor, for it is a pious and laudable act.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.1, Antiquities
items.quote: If the heir paid the ancestor’s debts, he did a pious and laudable act, beneficial for the departed soul as would be the endowment of a chantry.
items.conflict: Works cannot benefit the dead; salvation is not by works for the dead (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:26).
items.needs_role: heir (the person who succeeds to the dead man's lands and goods)

items.text: Pay wergild to the slain man’s children, brothers, uncles, and cousins; make atonement with them, for they have been wronged.
items.citation: History of English Law, VI.1, Antiquities
items.quote: The slain man’s brothers, uncles and cousins, as well as his children, have been wronged and atonement must be made with them.
items.conflict: Each person is responsible for his own sin; do not punish children for fathers' sins (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20); vengeance is the Lord's.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Honor your father's deathbed bequests and confirm them, lest his curse fall upon you.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, History of English Law, vol. 2, ch. VI § 3
items.quote: “a father’s curse” was a potent argument.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Reserve the bairns' part for your children; do not devise all your goods away from them.
items.citation: History of English Law, Book II, ch. VI, § 3 ('The Last Will')
items.quote: claims of children should set limits to a father’s testamentary power

items.text: Set aside your wife's part of your goods; let her share in your estate.
items.citation: History of English Law, Book II, ch. VI, § 3 ('The Last Will')
items.quote: wife’s part

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Leave to your wife her reasonable share of your movable goods.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law II, Ch. VI §3
items.quote: another to the wife if she be living

items.text: Leave to your children their reasonable share of your movable goods.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law II, Ch. VI §3
items.quote: one is to be left to the children (pueris)

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Provide for your younger brothers out of the inheritance that comes to you as the eldest son.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Bk. II, ch. VI, § 2, n.61
items.quote: lay stress on the duty of the eldest son to provide for his brothers.

items.text: Swear fealty to your elder sister when you share the ancestor's inheritance with her.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Bk. II, ch. VI, § 2, n.98
items.quote: the younger sisters swear fealty to the elder.

items.text: Collate the value of the fief to your brothers if you wish to share in the general inheritance.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Bk. II, ch. VI, § 2, n.65
items.quote: the eldest son, if he took the fief, had to 'collate' its value if he wished to share in the general inheritance.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Do not will away her lawful share; leave intact the half of your goods that belongs to her if you have no children, or her third if you have children.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3
items.quote: the wife takes a share

items.text: Do not will away their lawful share; leave intact for your children the half of your goods if there is no wife, or the third if there is a wife.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3
items.quote: the child or children a share

items.text: If you have already received an advancement from your father, bring it back into hotchpot before claiming your equal share, so that your brothers and sisters are not disadvantaged.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3
items.quote: bring back the advancement into hotchpot before claiming a bairn's right

items.text: If you claim a share in your father's movable goods, first collate the inheritance that has descended to you, so that your brothers and sisters receive equal portions.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 3
items.quote: the heir gets no share unless he will collate the inheritance

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Do not give away land in your last will without the consent of your heir, lest you dissipate the inheritance.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, ii.VI.3
items.quote: such a gift will hold good if made with the heir’s consent and confirmed by him.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Do not claim the land your father gave to a younger brother as long as any younger brother may claim it; be content with homage and service.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: He ought not to have it so long as there is any younger brother to claim it; enough for him that he will get homage and service.

items.text: Do not claim as heir the land you gave your son in fee; you must not be both lord and heir.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: The father is sent empty away and is told that he must not be both lord and heir.

items.text: Do not seek to inherit from your child; the law excludes all direct ancestors of the dead person.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance § 2
items.quote: an elementary rule of the law of inheritance excludes all direct ancestors of the dead man.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 2.: The Law of Descent

items.text: Allow your co-heir sister to demand and obtain a partition of the inherited land.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, Ch. VI, §2
items.quote: Any one of the parceners could demand a partition

items.text: Arrange the marriage of your ward, the young heiress, at the earliest possible moment.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, Ch. VI, §2
items.quote: her marriage was disposed of at the earliest possible moment

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Give to your spouse the conjugal duties that marriage requires.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Ch. VII §1
items.quote: each spouse has an action against the other spouse in which he or she can demand the prestation of conjugal duties.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Pay the debts of the dead man, using his chattels first, and if they are insufficient, make good the deficiency out of your own property.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters, Chapter VI: Inheritance § 3: The Last Will
items.quote: it is the heir who must pay the dead man’s debts

items.text: Do not dispose of your property, if burdened with debts, without the consent of your heir.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters, Chapter VI: Inheritance § 3: The Last Will
items.quote: A man who is burdened with debts cannot dispose of his property unless this be with the consent of his heir

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Treat as legitimate any child born to your wife during the marriage, even if you have doubts, for the law presumes him to be yours.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters, Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage
items.quote: every child born to a married woman is in law the legitimate child of her husband

items.text: If you are a widow, do not falsely claim to be with child in order to delay the heir's inheritance.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters, Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage
items.quote: our law was quick to suspect a fraud on the part of the widow who gave herself out to be with child

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Endow her at the church door, so that she may claim dower.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Book II, ch. 7, § 1
items.quote: No woman can claim dower unless she has been endowed at the church door.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Provide for your kinsfolk by your last will, giving them lands and goods.
items.citation: History of English Law, Ch. VI, § 3
items.quote: He gives his various lands specifically, providing for his kinsfolk

items.text: Protect the widow and the things left to her, and see that all bequests to her stand.
items.citation: History of English Law, Ch. VI, § 3
items.quote: protect my widow and the things that I leave to her... and that he aid that all the things may stand which I have bequeathed
items.needs_role: executor or guardian of the cwiðe

items.text: If a man dies without a will, distribute his property among his wife, children, and nearest kinsfolk, giving each their proper share.
items.citation: History of English Law, Ch. VI, § 3
items.quote: among the wife and children and nearest kinsfolk, to each the proper share
items.needs_role: lord or person directing the distribution

items.text: Do not infringe the testator's will; let his last words stand.
items.citation: History of English Law, Ch. VI, § 3
items.quote: the torments of hell are denounced against those who infringe it

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Remain faithful to the man to whom you gave present consent, and do not marry another.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII § 1
items.quote: after such a consent she could not and ought not to marry another

items.text: Keep your promise to marry; do not break faith or oath.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII § 1
items.quote: if he has given faith or sworn an oath, then a penance must be set him for the breach of his faith or of his oath.

items.text: When you give your daughter in marriage, obtain a priestly blessing.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII § 1
items.quote: him who gives away his daughter or kinswoman without a priestly benediction
items.needs_role: or kinsman giving away a daughter or kinswoman

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Live together as husband and wife; this duty ceases only on death or a divorce for fornication.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII: Family Law § 1: Marriage
items.quote: discharged the husband and wife from the duty of living together

items.text: Keep marital fidelity; avoid fornication, which alone grounds a separation from bed and board.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII: Family Law § 1: Marriage
items.quote: Such a divorce could be granted only 'for the cause of fornication'

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Obey him in all things not contrary to the law of God.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2
items.quote: she is bound to obey him in all that is not contrary to the law of God

items.text: Act as her guardian and head, protecting her interests.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2
items.quote: the husband is guardian as being the head of the wife

items.text: Be liable for her debts and wrongs, both before and during marriage.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2
items.quote: the husband is in effect liable to the whole extent of his property for debts incurred or wrongs committed by his wife

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Do not give a baby in marriage except under the pressure of some urgent need, such as the desire for peace.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Bk. II, ch.7 §1
items.quote: babies in the cradle were not to be given in marriage, except under the pressure of some urgent need, such as the desire for peace
items.conflict: Reformed teaching requires free consent of both parties; infant betrothal violates the child's future consent.

items.text: Obtain your father's consent before marrying while under age.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Bk. II, ch.7 §1
items.quote: with the consent of her father

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Do not make deathbed gifts to defraud your wife of the portion of goods that custom and law give her.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: condemn those who on their death-beds make gifts inter vivos for the purpose of defrauding ... their wives and children of the portions that belong to them

items.text: Do not make deathbed gifts to defraud your children of the portions that custom and law give them.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: condemn those who on their death-beds make gifts inter vivos for the purpose of defrauding ... their wives and children of the portions that belong to them

items.text: Leave to your wife the share of the goods that belongs to her by law or laudable custom.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: Elizabeth my wife shall have the share of goods that belongs to her by law or laudable custom.

items.text: Leave to your children the portions of goods that custom assigns to them.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: Antone my sonne and Betress my dowghter have their barne parts of my goodes after the lawe and custome of the cuntre

items.text: Pay to the widow the legitim due to her from the dead man's goods.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: The claim for legitim is therefore a claim against the executor, against one who is held accountable in the ecclesiastical court for a due administration.

items.text: Pay to each child the legitim due to him or her.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, vol. 2, Book II, c. 6, § 3
items.quote: On a testator's death his executor takes possession of the whole of his goods. He is bound to do this, for he has to pay the debts.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Endow your wife at the time of your espousals, whether with named lands not exceeding a third or, failing that, with a third of your lands.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: Every man is bound both by ecclesiastical and by temporal law to endow his spouse at the time of the espousals.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Remain with your husband and do not go off to live with another man; such conduct is adultery and forfeits your dower.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Chapter VII §1
items.quote: if a man’s wife in the life-time of her husband, of her own free will without objection or refusal, abides with another man, she is lying in adultery rather than in any due or lawful fashion

items.text: Do not give, grant, or quitclaim your wife to another man; the marriage bond remains and such a transfer is void.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Chapter VII §1
items.quote: the said Margaret was granted to the said William by the demise and delivery of the said John to remain with William for ever

items.text: Provide dower for her widowhood from your lands, unless she has forfeited it by eloping and adultery.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, Chapter VII §1
items.quote: dower that was due to her as widow of her first husband John de Camoys

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Contract no marriage with a kinsman within the forbidden degrees of consanguinity or affinity.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol.2, Book II, Ch.7, §1
items.quote: marriages within the fourth degree of consanguinity are null
items.conflict: Canonical degrees extend beyond Scripture's incest prohibitions; Reformed teaching adheres to biblical bounds.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Receive and treat her as your wife, and let her share the benefit of her own tenement.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: directing her husband to receive and treat her as his wife... share the benefit of her tenement

items.text: Do not drive your husband out of your own tenement or out of his tenement.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: If the wife drives the husband out of her tenement, or even out of his tenement

items.text: Do not alienate your wife's inheritance in fee simple; it must return to her or her heirs.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: A writ specially designed to enable the widow to recover the land thus alienated

items.text: Do not defraud your wife by collusive litigation to deprive her of her inheritance.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: it was a fraud for a husband to alienate his wife’s lands under cover of litigation

items.text: Do not hold your wife in contempt.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: a man is in gaol for “contemning” his wife

items.text: Remain faithful to your husband; do not elope with an adulterer.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, II.VII.2
items.quote: unless the wife has eloped with an adulterer

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Do not alienate the land set apart as her dower without her consent, lest she recover it after your death.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: If her husband alienates the land without her consent ... she can when her husband is dead recover that land

items.text: Assign her dower by metes and bounds within forty days after your father's death, if you are of age; otherwise your guardian must do it.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: To 'assign' the widow's dower was the duty of the heir or of his guardian: a duty to be performed within forty days after the husband's death.

items.text: If the heir is under age, assign the widow's dower by metes and bounds within forty days after her husband's death.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: assign the widow's dower was the duty of the heir or of his guardian: a duty to be performed within forty days

items.text: Give her her quarantine: let her remain in the principal house and be maintained at the cost of the estate for forty days after your father's death.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: During these forty days the widow had a right ... to remain in the principal house and to be maintained at the cost of the as yet undivided property

items.text: Endow her from the lands that descend to you, so far as they suffice, before she takes a third from a feoffee.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.2
items.quote: the heir confesses that other lands have come to him out of which he can sufficiently endow her, the feoffee will keep Blackacre and she will have judgment against the heir

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 3.: Infancy and Guardianship

items.text: Do not waste the infant ward's land, or the guardianship will be forfeited.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, ii, ch. vii, § 3
items.quote: an action for waste can be brought by the infant against the guardian, and, if the waste is proved, the guardianship will be forfeited

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 4.: Intestacy

items.text: Distribute the goods of a kinsman who dies intestate for the good of his soul, as the church directs.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, bk. II, ch. VI, § 4 (Intestacy)
items.quote: his chattels shall be distributed by the hands of his next kinsfolk and friends under the supervision of the church
items.conflict: The Bible teaches that after death comes judgment (Heb. 9:27) and that no work done by the living can benefit the dead; salvation is by grace through faith alone.

items.text: Do not prevent access to a dying kinsman for spiritual counsel and the making of his will.
items.citation: History of English Law, vol. 2, bk. II, ch. VI, § 4 (Intestacy)
items.quote: the brother, who was heir, and the wife, wishing to have all, would not allow any one to have access to the sick man

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Yield to him the possession and profits of all your lands for his lifetime once a child has been born.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife
items.quote: the husband holds “according to the custom of the kingdom”

items.text: Allow your mother's second husband to hold her lands for his life, even though you are the heir.
items.citation: History of English Law, Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife
items.quote: it is given to a second husband, who can thereby keep out a son of the first marriage from his inheritance.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Provide for your wife in your will; she has a portion secured to her by law.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.vi.3
items.quote: His wife and children, as we shall hereafter see, have portions secured to them by law

items.text: Provide for your children in your will; they have portions secured to them by law.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.vi.3
items.quote: His wife and children, as we shall hereafter see, have portions secured to them by law

items.text: As executrix, arrange his burial and funeral feast as he directed.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.vi.3
items.quote: Elaborate instructions will sometimes be given for the burial; about the tapers that are to burn around the bier, and the funeral feast.

items.text: As executrix, expend the residue of his estate for the good of his soul, as he directed.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.vi.3
items.quote: when he does make a residuary gift, he frequently makes it in favour of his executors and bids them expend it for his benefit
items.conflict: No purgatory; the dead's fate is fixed (Heb 9:27); money cannot secure pardon.

items.text: If your mother dies before the will is performed, take her place as executor and complete it.
items.citation: History of English Law, II.vi.3
items.quote: his wife is to be his attorney, and, if she dies before his will is performed, his son is to take her place

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 1.: Antiquities

items.text: Before removing your wife from her kinsmen's district, give them security that you will treat her well.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Inheritance § 1
items.quote: giving them security that he would treat her well

items.text: Stand answerable for her wrongs; do not bring vengeance on her husband's innocent family.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Inheritance § 1
items.quote: if she committed homicide, vengeance was not to be taken on 'the innocent family' of her husband.

items.text: Contribute your due share of the wer: paternal kin two-thirds, maternal kin one-third.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Inheritance § 1
items.quote: the paternal kinsfolk pay and receive two-thirds, the maternal kinsfolk one-third of the wer

items.text: Avenge your father's death, going out with your brothers and paternal uncles.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Inheritance § 1
items.quote: Along with his brothers and paternal uncles a man goes out to avenge his father's death
items.conflict: Vengeance is the Lord's; love your enemies.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 3.: Infancy and Guardianship

items.text: Exercise the guardianship as a trust for the ward's benefit, not merely as a profitable right.
items.citation: History of English Law, VII.3
items.quote: A statute was required to convert the profitable rights of the guardian in socage into a trust to be exercised for the infant’s benefit.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Provide your wife sufficient maintenance; do not starve or maltreat her.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: directing the sheriff to provide her with a sufficient maintenance out of the lands of a husband who had refused to behave as a husband should

items.text: Do not kill, maim, or use violence beyond reasonable chastisement against your wife.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: If she went in fear of any violence exceeding a reasonable chastisement, he could be bound with sureties to keep the peace

items.text: Honor your wife's purchase of necessaries on your credit; provide for household needs.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: her power to 'pledge her husband's credit' for necessaries

items.text: Do not enter religion without your spouse's consent; both must desire to leave the world.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: permit a husband or wife to enter religion unless both of them are desirous of leaving the world

items.text: Do not dispose of land held jointly without your spouse's concurrence; act together in any conveyance.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: Neither of the spouses has anything; both of them have all.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Pay fifty shillings to her guardian and buy his consent.
items.citation: History of English Law, 7.1
items.quote: If a man forcibly abducts a maiden, let him pay 50 shillings to him to whom she belongs and then buy the consent of him to whom she belongs.

items.text: Do not give your daughter in marriage without priestly blessing.
items.citation: History of English Law, 7.1
items.quote: ut nullus filiam suam vel cognatam det alicui absque benedictione sacerdotali — that no one give his daughter or kinswoman to anyone without priestly blessing.

items.text: Each must render the conjugal debt to the other.
items.citation: History of English Law, 7.1
items.quote: l’obligation du devoir conjugal, non seulement dans le forum internum, mais encore devant le forum externum — the obligation of the conjugal duty, not only in the internal forum, but also before the external forum.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Leave to your widow the share of your chattels that law allows; do not deprive her of it by testamentary disposition.
items.citation: History of English Law, Book II, Ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: our old law securing to the widow an aliquot share of chattels of which her husband cannot deprive her by testamentary disposition

items.text: If she dies intestate, distribute a share of the chattels for the good of her soul.
items.citation: History of English Law, Book II, Ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: When the wife dies intestate, ought one-third, or perhaps one-half, of the chattels to be distributed for the good of her soul?
items.conflict: No offering or alms can benefit the dead; salvation is by faith in Christ alone.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 4.: Intestacy

items.text: Distribute his part for the good of his soul in pious works as you think best according to God and good conscience.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance §4
items.quote: The dead's part they are to distribute for the good of his soul in such pious works as they shall think best according to God and good conscience.
items.conflict: Praying for the dead is unbiblical; the dead cannot be helped after death (Luke 16:26).

items.text: Assign to her the widow's one-third share of the residue according to the custom of the realm.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance §4
items.quote: assigning one to his widow Margaret

items.text: Assign to the children their one-third share of the residue according to the custom of the realm.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance §4
items.quote: assigning one to the children 'according to the custom of the realm of England.'

items.text: Retain the children's share as curators and guardians until they come of full age.
items.citation: History of English Law, Inheritance §4
items.quote: The bairns' part they are to retain as curators and guardians until the children are of full age.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 3.: Infancy and Guardianship

items.text: Do not sell him into slavery without his consent once he is seven years old.
items.citation: History of English Law before Edward I, vol.2, Family Law §3
items.quote: An older boy could not be sold without his consent.
items.conflict: Selling children into slavery is forbidden (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 5:8).

items.text: Do not answer for his inherited land in court; bring him to answer as an independent person.
items.citation: History of English Law before Edward I, vol.2, Family Law §3
items.quote: the father ought not to represent the land in the consequent litigation; he will 'pray aid' of his child

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Do not marry anyone within the forbidden degrees of affinity, whether through your spouse or through sexual intercourse.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §1
items.quote: All my wife’s or my mistress’ blood kinswomen are connected with me by way of affinity.
items.conflict: Prohibits marriage beyond biblical degrees; treats illicit intercourse as creating marriage-like bonds.
items.needs_role: affine (one related through spouse or sexual intercourse)

items.text: Do not marry your godmother.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §1
items.quote: the godson may marry neither his godmother
items.conflict: Spiritual kinship is not a biblical marriage impediment.

items.text: Do not marry your godmother’s daughter.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §1
items.quote: nor his godmother’s daughter
items.conflict: Spiritual kinship is not a biblical marriage impediment.

items.text: Do not marry without your guardian’s consent, and do not reject a suitable marriage he tenders.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §1
items.quote: punishing the ward who married without the consent of the guardian in chivalry or rejected a 'convenable marriage' which he tendered

items.text: Do not make a profit for yourself out of the marriage of your ward.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §1
items.quote: A statute of 1267 forbad the guardian in socage to make a profit for himself out of the marriage of his ward.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Do not bar her dower right in land without her consent.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: the husband could not, as a general rule, bar the wife’s right without her consent

items.text: Do not use collusive actions to defeat her dower claims.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: the court in Bracton’s day was doing what it could to suppress this fraud, for fraud it was

items.text: Endow her at marriage as you declared at the church door.
items.citation: History of English Law, ch. VII, § 2
items.quote: the wife is endowed, because the husband has said at the church door that he endows her

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 1.: Marriage

items.text: Do not give her in marriage to a man she dislikes; gain her consent.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: Even Cnut had to forbid that a woman should be sold to a man whom she disliked.

items.text: Stipulate on her behalf for an honourable treatment as wife and widow; secure her settlement.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: the more essential matter is that they should stipulate on her behalf for an honourable treatment as wife and widow.

items.text: Treat her as an honourable consort and yoke-fellow, not as a chattel or unequal partner.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: An honourable position as her husband’s consort and yoke-fellow was assured to her by solemn contract.

items.text: Give her the morning-gift and the dower as promised at betrothal; make and keep the settlement.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: He declares, and he gives security for, the morning-gift which she shall receive if she “chooses his will” and the dower that she shall enjoy if she outlives him.

items.text: As her protector, guard and care for her in all things.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: it was a sale of the mund, the protectorship, over the woman

items.text: Reverence and obey him as your lord and elder.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: He became her “elder”— her senior, her seigneur, we may say,—and her lord

items.text: Accept the marriage arranged by your parents; do not obstinately refuse the man to whom you were betrothed.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: the church held that the parents of the espoused girl might give her to another man, if she obstinately refused the man to whom she had been betrothed.
items.conflict: Forces marriage against her persistent refusal; overrides individual consent (cf. 1 Cor 7:39).

items.text: Be faithful to your husband; do not commit adultery.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: The adulterous wife, unless her offence be public, is to be handed over to the bishop for judgment.

items.text: Be faithful to your wife; do not commit adultery.
items.citation: Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, Family Law, Marriage
items.quote: The adulterous husband is to be denied every Christian right until he satisfies the bishop.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 3.: Infancy and Guardianship

items.text: Do not claim any share of the paternal inheritance, for it belongs entirely to the eldest son.
items.citation: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II, Chapter VII, § 3.
items.quote: The eldest son absolutely excludes his brothers from the paternal inheritance

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Yield to your husband the ownership of all chattels you bring or receive during marriage; they are his.
items.citation: History of English Law, II, ch. VII § 2
items.quote: The marriage transfers the ownership of the bride’s chattels to the husband, and whatever chattels come to the wife during the marriage belong to the husband.

items.text: Do not make a will of any goods without your husband's consent; his permission is required.
items.citation: History of English Law, II, ch. VII § 2
items.quote: a woman who is under the power of a husband cannot make a will without the consent of her husband.

items.text: Provide for her after your death: she must receive half your chattels if there is no child, or a third if a child survives; dispose only of your own share.
items.citation: History of English Law, II, ch. VII § 2
items.quote: assures to the wife a half, or if there is a child alive, a third of the chattels.

items.text: Do not dispose of her clothes and ornaments by will; they are hers and must not pass under your testament.
items.citation: History of English Law, II, ch. VII § 2
items.quote: If the wife survives the husband, these things will not pass under his testament; the wife’s claim upon them will prevail against his legatees.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Do not alienate your land during marriage without your husband's concurrence by fine.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: The wife has during the marriage no power to alienate her land without her husband's concurrence.

items.text: Do not alienate your own land so as to bar your wife's dower unless she consents by fine.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: the husband cannot alienate his own land so as to bar his wife's right of dower, unless this is done with her concurrence

items.text: Submit to your husband's taking possession of your movables and suing for debts due to you.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: the husband is entitled to take possession of and thereby to make his own whatever movables she becomes entitled to during the marriage

items.text: Make no will without your husband's consent, which he may revoke any time before probate.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: Without his consent she can make no will, and any consent that he may have given is revocable at any time before the will is proved.

items.text: Do not dispose of your wife's chattels real by your will; if not alienated in your lifetime, they are hers if she survives.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: the husband, though he can alienate his wife's 'chattel real' inter vivos, cannot dispose of it by his will.

items.text: Do not give away your wife's paraphernalia by will; they remain hers after your death.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law §2
items.quote: but he cannot give them away by will

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 2.: Husband and Wife

items.text: Treat her well and govern her without doing bodily harm; do not oppress or abuse her.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: he will treat and govern the said A well and decently, and will not do nor procure any damage or evil to her body

items.text: Do not impede your wife in making her will; allow her free and customary testamentary disposition of her own goods.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: ne quis alicuius solutae mulieris vel coniugatae, alienae vel propriae, impediat vel perturbet, seu impediri aut perturbari faciat seu procuret, iustam et consuetam testamenti liberam factionem

items.text: Be subject to your husband's governance, as one under his rod.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: quia fuit sub virga viri sui

items.text: Do not defraud your wife in dealings with her land; obtain her genuine consent and do not impersonate or deceive her.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: a husband who has fraudulently levied a fine of his wife’s land, by producing in court another woman who personated his wife

items.text: Do not dispose of your wife's separate land; it is hers to control.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: ipsa habuit terram suam separatam et liberam a dominatu et potestate Bernulfi mariti sui... ita ut ipse de ea nec donationem, nec venditionem facere, nec foris-facere posset

items.text: Obtain your wife's free consent before conveying her land, except in urgent necessity.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: except perhaps in case of urgent necessity, it is requisite that there should be some proof of her free action

items.text: Do not despise or neglect your wife; treat her according to marital law.
items.citation: History of English Law, Family Law § 2 Husband and Wife
items.quote: captus pro contumacia sua eo quod contempsit uxorem suam

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VI: Inheritance · § 3.: The Last Will

items.text: Do not dispose of your goods beyond the payment of your debts without your heir's consent.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: Si vero fuerit debitis oneratus is qui testamentum facere proponit, nihil de rebus suis (extra debitorum acquietationem) praeter sui heredis consensum disponere potest. — If he who intends to make a will is burdened with debts, he cannot dispose of anything of his goods (except payment of debts) without his heir's consent.

items.text: Pay the debts of the deceased; if his goods do not suffice, make up the deficiency from your own property.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: Si vero non sufficiunt res defuncti ad debita persolvenda, tunc quidem heres ipse defectum ipsum de suo tenetur adimplere — But if the goods of the deceased do not suffice to pay debts, then the heir himself is bound to make up the deficiency from his own property.

items.text: Do not oppose or disturb my donation; honor the bequests of the deceased.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: prohibeo ex parte Dei et mea ne quis heredum meorum huic donationi meae contraire vel eam in aliquo perturbare praesumat. — I forbid on God's part and mine that any of my heirs presume to oppose this my donation or disturb it in any way.

items.text: Leave your wife her lawful share of your goods; dispose only of your own third.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: uxoresque et liberi coniugatorum suis portionibus de consuetudine vel de iure ipsis debitis irrecuperabiliter defraudantur — the wives and children of married men are irrecoverably defrauded of their portions due to them by custom or law.

items.text: Leave your children their lawful share; do not defraud them of their portion.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: liberorum et suarum uxorum, qui et quae tam de iure quam de consuetudine certam quotam dictorum bonorum habere deberent — children and their wives ought by law and custom to have a certain share of the said goods.

items.text: Provide for your younger children in your will, so they are not left without sufficient provision.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: whereby many persons are disabled from making sufficient provision for their younger children.

items.text: Carry your lord's body to the place he appointed for burial, as he commanded.
items.citation: Hist. Eng. Law, Inheritance, Last Will
items.quote: Praecepit etiam suis omnibus, contestans fidem quam ei debebant, ut suum corpus ad abbatiam suam quam Colecestriae construxerat deferrent. — He also commanded all his men, adjuring them by the faith they owed him, to carry his body to his abbey which he had built at Colchester.

work: The History of English Law before the Time of Edward I, vol. 2, Book II chapters
heading: Chapter VII: Family Law · § 3.: Infancy and Guardianship

items.text: Assert the claim of a female relative in court; let her do the swearing.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii.7.3
items.quote: a woman’s claim is asserted in court by a kinsman, but she does the swearing.

items.text: Sue a wasteful guardian on behalf of your minor child.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii.7.3
items.quote: aliquis parens vel amicus qui de vasto sequatur pro minore

items.text: As guardian, sue or defend for your ward in court, for the infant cannot act for himself.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii.7.3
items.quote: At common law, infants could neither sue nor defend, except by guardian.

items.text: Produce the infant in your keeping before the justices when summoned.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii.7.3
items.quote: tunc summoneatur ille in cuius manu fuerit et cuius consilio ductus quod sit et habeat [infantem coram iusticiariis] tali die.

items.text: As father or guardian by nature, bring the writ against anyone who abducts the child.
items.citation: Pollock & Maitland, Hist. Eng. Law, ii.7.3
items.quote: The writ for a father or other 'guardian by nature' against the abducer of the child.
